name: PSI
seoDesc: PSI: work out your result from the age. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary:
The PSI calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports the result immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer.

Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the PSI calculator work?
sections.html:
The PSI calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex and what has been observed about the patient when examined?); then you type in the age.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as female and male. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A number, expressed in years.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Nursing home resident”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “History of renal disease”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Liver disease”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Neoplasm”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “CHF (congestive heart failure)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Altered mental status”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Pleural effusion (visible on X-ray)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Respiratory rate ≥ 30 breaths/min”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Pulse ≥ 125 BPM”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Blood pressure: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Temperature <95 °F or >103.8 °F (<35 °C or >39.9 °C)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Blood Urea Nitrogen: BUN ≥ 30 Mg/d l (11 mmol/L)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Hematocrit < 30%”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Sodium < 130 mmol/L (or 130 mEq/L)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Glucose ≥ 250 Mg/d l (14 mmol/L)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “pH < 7.35”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Partial pressure of oxygen: pO₂ < 60 mmHg (8 kPa)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A number, expressed in points.

19 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the PSI calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Celebrovascular Disease=PSI ÷ PORT − age − what has been observed about the patient when examined? − select the laboratory findings that apply to the patient... − chf − glucose − hematocrit − liver Disease − neoplasm − please select all that apply to the patient... − partial Pressure − ph − pleural Effusion − pulse − renal Disease − respiratory rate − sex − sodium − systolic bp − temperature

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The PSI calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the age — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the PSI calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, which is 20 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (19 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the PSI calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
